title: What do you think defines an “arthouse/art film” aesthetic?

commenti.body:
In college, I wrote about ‘distanciation’ - essentially what defines an art house movie is that it in some way creates a distance between the film and viewer; thus making the viewer aware on *some level* that this film has a point of view, is more than just the author-less story that comes out of Hollywood. 

Creating distance can be done by altering the film itself - as with Godard’s work in inventing the jump cut, or in choosing to make your film black & white, say. This distance can be created by making your actors act in a strange way - Kubrick and his 100 takes. Or it could be in subverting genre convention - the way David Lynch movies start as some sort of noir and end up on a metaphysical plain.

Distanciation is a very broad term, essentially meant to encompass anything that might make a movie an ‘art house’ movie.

Thank you so much for all this detail! This makes so much sense. The write up I found the arthouse definition for was on “The Birds”, which the writer calls Hitchcock’s only, nearly, through and through arthouse film, that it’s a loose plot based on abstraction and metaphysical yearning and has a certain distanced formalism that shapes it as something removed from just pop cinema. Would you say certain formalist care is a major characteristic?

I was going to say, I think I define it more by what it doesn't do. It doesn't prioritize being accessible or put audience satisfaction ahead of artistic intent. With a mainstream film, the filmmakers are expected to meet the audience where they are at. With art house, the audience is expected to meet the filmmaker where they are.

Oh for sure. ‘Formalism’ really means, in a sense, to place cinematic gesture above just conveying a narrative. Like in Wes Anderson’s films - often the idea of the story is quite simple - but his presentation becomes so complicated it can be thrilling (or a chore) to keep track. On the other hand Spielberg creates amazing shots, breathtaking - but 99% of the time he’s just trying to convey as much info as he can as quickly as he can. So his formal innovations are actually in service of economy - telling a complicated story quickly and efficiently. The exact opposite of what Anderson is doing. 

I personally would argue that Hitchcock has several distanciated films, though not always due to formal ambition. Rope - the whole schtick is its one take. Rear Window? All - 1 apartment. Vertigo is structurally distanciated but formally more straightforward than the birds

Very interesting observations on Anderson Vs. Spielberg, I think the latter director is more of a “populist” one because of that economy. I haven’t seen all of his work, but I think by and large even with his great skill/mastery he isn’t called an “arty” director. 

I’ve been watching the films of Mike Nichols lately, a man who reshaped what “auteur” meant in many ways, and while he made great/brilliant works until the 2000’s he was shaping his movies with much more arty formalism at the beginning of his career than later. 

And Hitchcock definitely used arthouse “devices” in other films and used space beyond conventional ways, but I think The Birds is where his formal and structural ambitions melded together the most, with probably Vertigo following. It’s no surprise that Truffaut was a huge fan of The Birds because it likely reflected that abstraction of the FNW.

Yeah, I agree with all that. Nichols is interesting because, yeah, he became more interested in supporting actors and character development over the years. The industry also changed so much - he wasn’t the kinda big name who could mess around w art and work regularly, necessarily, in the 80s and 90s.

The auteur theory is interesting, I think, because it allows for a deeper reading of the narrative in many ways. I studied Marxist film theory, and came to think of a film more as a product, with the film production being more akin to a startup company than a director-lead artist troupe. 

Which is simply to say that - as you read films more deeply, know that there are other ways of doing so. None are better than the others necessarily, they just lead to different insights.

I don’t know if it wasn’t that he couldn’t stretch his artistic legs, after all he was given big budgets and garnering acclaim/making hits into the 90s, I just think that visually, while never slack, he became less interested in that arty distancing and made more “commercially” formal works without sacrificing his authorial through-line. 

Did the Marxist film theory sorta of disillusion you some on the artistic realm of cinema, or that it’s something that needs to be more strived for as opposed to it falling in your lap?

That last paragraph and line is so beautiful and very helpful for the films I want to make. I have many thoughts and they lead back to discovering those ineffable insights that only cinema can manifest.

Luckily we have an arthouse cinema downtown. They only employ pretentious spoiled brats. I don’t think art house films are necessarily pretentious, but they’re crafted in a way that attracts viewers who yearn for… deeper meaning in storytelling… people who appreciate symbolism and poetic ideas. Art inspires people to think. One of my most prized possessions is a painting of Elvis just before he died. The artist depicts him holding a microphone, in a white jumpsuit, covered in sweat. It causes thoughts, makes you wonder. Arthouse does the same.

I don’t think the inherent nature of arthouse is that the films are way too heady. Some audience members just never grow up. Never get an education on art or arthouse. They’re playing Clockwatchers downtown at the arthouse cinema. Others might see that poster, then drive across town to see Kung Fu Panda 4.

Arthouse is like art, it causes the viewer to wonder about the meaning of things. It doesn’t feed it to you like Wild Hogs. Rachmaninov piano concerto number 2 is a symphonic story of a man’s battle with overcoming depression. A proper education in music gives you the gift of feeling each emotion. So does an education in arthouse in order to have fun and try to figure out what the director is saying.

Thanks for introducing me to that term, I need to research it a bit more. 

With all art there is a push/pull between the subject and object, which basically comes from heightened formalism.

An art house film will have you constantly moving between an awareness of the film as an aesthetic *thing* and (ideally) the subject matter. 

An artist tends to draw attention to the "object" of their medium in some way to elevate it beyond the "illustrative" (which in film would be pure documentary).

In a review of **Chungking Express** the American critic Roger Ebert suggested that "this is the kind of film you relate to if you love film itself, rather than its surface aspects such as story and stars."  Perhaps this remark is helpful in trying to determine what an 'arthouse' or 'serious' film aesthetic consists of?  He goes on to say "a film like (**Chungking Express**) is largely a cerebral experience: You enjoy it because of what you know about film, not what it knows about life".

I think it's a nebulous concept that has more to do with positioning ones self against and opposed to whatever the mainstream look is.

Combine that with the ingenuity and corner cutting necessary within the limits of (usually) much smaller budget, and you end up with the current look of art house.

Of course, we are now many generations of art house films deep, so now you also add in the aesthetics of past art house movements informing the new, by way of either meeting or subverting expectations of what an art house film is "supposed" to look like.

It’s a bit confusing for me, like is Taxi Driver art house, is Raging Bull art house? I’d consider David Lynch arthouse but not Blue Velvet, I’d consider The Shining arthouse but not Dr Strangelove. I feel like my idea of art house is pretty specific in terms of plot and theme, where plot is forgone for style or atmosphere.

Arthouse films seem like the anti "mainstream movies", that is, anything that wouldn't be considered something an average American would watch, and sometimes is catered to being broadly popular.

For the longest time, foreign movies fit the bill, but they were critically acclaimed, partly because it was expensive to make blockbuster movies in other countries, but now, countries like India have done it for a while (e.g., RRR).   RRR could be called arthouse, but is it?

I think you get into truly art-y movies when you decide not to explain every detail to an audience (though some of that goes on) or to make a movie popular.  If you read the plot to Memoria by Apitchatpong Weerasethakul, it seems like a strange movie indeed.  What is it's point?  How could this ever make money?  In a way, Weerasethakul is lucky because he's a critically acclaimed director that's internationally known from a country that doesn't produce a lot of movies that get worldwide attention, so he gets to make his kinds of movies.  In a different country, he might not be able to achieve this.

I think it's almost easier to define it like "anti mainstream" rather than something arthouse movies have in common.  Is Moon an arthouse movie?  Why?  It's science fiction.  Sure, no big explosions, but it isn't hard to follow.  Yet, not many people saw it.  Or Sunshine.
I think mostly people do consider BV arthouse, and id agree.
